terms.comment: Latin usually turns an English “immediate” into an adverb with the verb: an immediate answer is an answer given at once (statim respondēre), and Livy’s plenty “at once bred boredom”. See at once.

evidence: Cic. Div. 2.122: praesēns poena, instant punishment (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Clu. 34: praesentī pecūniā, with ready money (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of what is done or paid on the spot. Its first sense is present, in person, at hand (praesēns tēcum ēgī, Cic. Fam. 2.7.4), and of time, the present (see current).

phrases.latin: fēcit statim, ut fit, fastīdium cōpia
phrases.english: plenty, as usually happens, bred immediate boredom

phrases.latin: nīl spernat auris, nec tamen crēdat statim
phrases.english: let the ear scorn nothing, and yet believe nothing at once

sources: Lewis & Short: statim · Lewis & Short: praesum (praesens) · Lewis & Short: mora
